intro: Milan's remarkable trees are rarely medieval; the city rebuilt itself too many times, and around itself even more, for old wood to survive by accident. What lasted here did so because an institution kept records (a university's ginkgo pair, brought from China in 1775), a neighbourhood organised (a paulownia a Brera committee saved from a car park in 2016), or a park changed its job entirely (a horse-racing track that became a school for sick children in 1919 and kept its oaks). Twenty-one trees, and almost every one owes its survival to a specific human decision.
meta_description: Milan's twenty-two remarkable trees, from a 1775 ginkgo pair to a plane tree a Brera committee saved from demolition in 2016.
question_answer: Milan's oldest tree is one of a pair of ginkgo trees in the Orto Botanico di Brera, planted in 1775 when the garden's founders imported them directly from China. Both are now around 250 years old and grow a few steps from the garden's 18th-century greenhouse on Via Brera 28.
question_meta: Milan's oldest tree is a 250-year-old ginkgo pair at the Orto Botanico di Brera, planted from Chinese seed in 1775. Its story, plus twenty-one more trees.
question_context: Milan has never been an easy city for an old tree to survive in. Wars, plague and relentless nineteenth and twentieth century redevelopment levelled most of what predates them, so almost nothing on this list is medieval. The one clear exception is the university's own ginkgo biloba pair, a male and a female planted together in 1775 when Abbot Fulgenzio Vitman was building the Orto Botanico di Brera for Empress Maria Theresa's new medical faculty, importing seed directly from China less than two decades after the species had reached Europe at all. Italy's monumental tree registry calculates their age from growth data at 235 years, a little short of the 251 years a straight planting-date count would give; this page states both rather than picking one, since the gap is exactly the kind of rounding error that comes from measuring a slow grower by two different methods. Either way, they are Milan's oldest trees by a wide margin over anything else here, and the garden marked their joint 250th anniversary with a public conference in March 2026.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Milan?
faq.a: One of a pair of ginkgo trees in the Orto Botanico di Brera, planted in 1775 from seed brought directly from China. Depending on the calculation method, the pair is 235 to 251 years old, the oldest documented trees in the city by a wide margin.

faq.q: Are Milan's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: All twenty-two on this list are free. Unlike Rome or Florence, none of Milan's most remarkable trees stand inside a paid garden or monument; the closest things to a ticket are Parco Trotter's restricted opening hours, since its grounds double as a working school, and the park of Villa Marietti Radice Fossati, where the Archdevil hackberry grows: the city asks for the discretion due to an inhabited place, because people live in the villa buildings, and says the gate may be passed to visit the park.

faq.q: Why does Milan have so few genuinely ancient trees compared to Rome or Florence?
faq.a: Milan lacks the long-running institutional gardens, papal villas and monastery grounds that protected old trees elsewhere in Italy. Almost everything on this list was planted deliberately within the last two centuries, inside parks built from scratch or squares redesigned after the city's rapid nineteenth and twentieth century growth.

faq.q: Has Milan lost any of its historic trees recently?
faq.a: Yes. A widely loved 200-year-old red oak known as the Quercia di Montale fell in October 2019 during heavy rain; its trunk is preserved in place rather than removed. A plane tree planted in 1773 at Villa Litta, once one of the city's oldest, was felled in 2015 after a fungal disease; a cross-section of its trunk is displayed inside the villa.

trees.name: Il Sacerdote

location.address: Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, Corso Venezia 55, 20121 Milano

trees.story: For years, gardeners in Porta Venezia's park called this tree a metasequoia and had the genus wrong before anyone checked properly. It is in fact a bald cypress, one of the first ever planted in Milan, native to the swamps of the American South rather than to any part of Italy, and one of very few conifers anywhere that drops its needles for winter, the trait that gives the whole species its English name. Standing roughly 35 metres tall with a trunk 6.2 metres around, it grows at the edge of the artificial lake inside the Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, Milan's oldest public park, opened in 1784 on land a Habsburg duke gave up for prisoners to landscape. Other cypresses share its stretch of water, but this is the tallest and widest of the whole stand, the reason the Milanese writer and forest scholar Tiziano Fratus nicknamed it Il Sacerdote, the priest, for the way its bare winter branches spread like a robe. Its roots, like those of every bald cypress in wet ground, throw up woody knees above the waterline to breathe, a feature visitors often mistake for stumps. At around 156 years old it predates the park's nineteenth century English-garden makeover and has outlasted the zoo that once shared these grounds, dismantled in 1992.
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Porta Venezia (M1)

best_time.label: October into November, when its needles turn rust orange before falling

trees.notes: Age corroborated within a consistent range by a second, independent source (josway.it gives 150-200 years); no real dispute, RAMI's 156-year figure used as the point estimate. A candidate photo (Cipresso calvo a primavera, dettaglio.jpg, CC BY-SA 4.0, geotagged about 15m from this entry's own coordinates) was viewed directly this pass and rejected: it's an upward view showing at least two or three separate cypress trunks close together, consistent with the story's own note that several cypresses share this stretch of water, so it cannot be confirmed as Il Sacerdote specifically rather than a neighbour.

trees.name: Platano di Indro

location.address: Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, Corso Venezia 55, 20121 Milano

trees.story: The largest plane tree in Milan does not grow tall so much as it grows sideways, in every direction at once. Named for Indro Montanelli, the journalist the park was rededicated to in 2002, it stands about 50 metres from his statue with a trunk 8.36 metres around, the widest of any plane in the city, rising from a short, irregular, deeply fluted base that splits almost at ground level into at least five major limbs, each thick enough to be a trunk of its own. The effect, according to arborists who have surveyed it, is closer to a vase held open than to the single straight column most plane trees grow into. No planting record survives, ordinary for a park redesigned twice since 1784 and never catalogued tree by tree until recently, so its age can only be guessed at from girth: somewhere in its second century, possibly its third. What is documented is who lives in it. Ring-necked parakeets, an escaped-pet species now breeding wild across Milan, nest in cavities high in the crown, adding flashes of tropical green to a tree already too disorderly to look properly manicured. Visitors chasing the statue for a photograph rarely look up at what is standing over it.
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Porta Venezia (M1)
trees.notes: No planting date or age documented anywhere found; age range is a wide, honest estimate from trunk girth alone, bounded loosely by the park's 1784 founding. A candidate Commons photo (Platano_secolare_ai_Giardini_Montanelli.jpg) was viewed and rejected: its caption identifies it only as 'a centuries-old plane tree' in the gardens generally, and the park holds several large planes, so it could not be confirmed as this specific, individually surveyed specimen.

trees.name: Bagolaro dei Giardini Montanelli

location.address: Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, Corso Venezia 55, 20121 Milano

trees.story: Milan calls this species spaccasassi, the stone-splitter, for roots strong enough to crack paving, and this hackberry has had over a century and a half to test the claim against the paths of the city's oldest public park. Standing 27 metres tall with a trunk 4.24 metres around, it is one of seven trees the city has formally recognised as monumental within the Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, sharing that status with the plane and the cypress a short walk away. Celtis australis is native across the Mediterranean and was planted widely in nineteenth century Milan for the same reason it thrives today: almost nothing bothers it, not soot, not drought, not the compacted soil under a park crossed by tens of thousands of people a week. Its small, dark, cherry-like fruit ripens in autumn and draws blackbirds rather than people, who mostly walk past a tree with none of the visible drama of its more contorted neighbours. Italy's monumental tree registry puts its age at 164 years, calculated from growth data rather than any surviving planting record, the only figure any source gives; treated here as an estimate rather than a settled fact.
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Porta Venezia (M1)
trees.notes: The 164-year age figure comes from RAMI's registry only; the second source (comune.milano.it) confirms species, location and monumental status but not that specific number, so the age is flagged as single-sourced.

trees.name: Il Ginkgo dell'Orto Botanico di Brera

location.address: Orto Botanico di Brera, Via Brera 28, 20121 Milano

trees.story: Behind Palazzo Brera's courtyard grows a pair of trees older than the idea of Italy itself: a male and a female ginkgo, planted together in 1775 when Empress Maria Theresa's new botanical garden was barely a year old, grown from seed carried directly from China less than two decades after the species had reached Europe at all. Ginkgo biloba is often called a living fossil, essentially unchanged for over 200 million years and the sole survivor of a family that once grew alongside dinosaurs; this pair is a comparative sapling by that measure, but at somewhere between 235 and 251 years old, depending on whether growth-ring calculation or the garden's own planting record is trusted, they are the oldest documented trees in Milan by a wide margin. In March 2026 the university marked their joint 250th anniversary with a public conference built entirely around the two trees. Every November their fan-shaped leaves turn a uniform gold and drop within days rather than fading gradually, briefly carpeting the beds around them. Entry to the garden is free, a rarity among Milan's oldest sites, down a courtyard most visitors to the Pinacoteca next door never think to enter.
trees.access: Free entry, Orto Botanico di Brera (Mon-Sat, hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Lanza (M2) or Montenapoleone (M3)

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn uniform gold and drop within days

trees.notes: Age genuinely disputed between two calculation methods: RAMI's registry gives 235 years from growth data, while the garden's own 250th-anniversary material (2026) implies a 251-year planting-date count from 1775. Presented as a range rather than asserting either. Two Commons garden photos were checked (Brera Botanical Garden - 4.jpg, Orto botanico Brera a Milano 319.jpg) and rejected: neither caption identifies a ginkgo specifically among the garden's roughly 300 plant beds. Photo status corrected 2026-07-30: a CC BY iNaturalist observation (obs 288159360, codrin_bucur, June 2025, geotagged within a few metres of this entry's own coordinates, observer's own note reads "From 1775" matching this entry's planting date exactly) had been rejected by a 2026-07-28 session as showing "vine-like leaves climbing the trunk, not the unmistakable fan-shaped leaves." Downloaded and viewed the full-resolution original directly this session: the canopy filling most of the frame (upper left, upper right, along the branches) is unmistakably ginkgo, dozens of the distinctive notched fan-shaped leaves visible throughout. A separate, smaller cluster of grayer, rounder leaves partway up the trunk, likely an incidental vine growing on the tree, is what the prior session's description matches, not the canopy as a whole. Approved on this session's direct look; noting the reversal plainly since it corrects a specific prior call.

trees.name: La Catalpa della Guastalla

location.address: Giardini della Guastalla, Via Francesco Sforza 23, 20122 Milano

trees.story: Milan's oldest public garden, laid out in 1555 for a countess who did not live to see it finished, keeps its strangest tree behind a baroque fish pond nobody expects to find in the middle of the city. This catalpa, a North American species imported to Europe for ornamental foliage rather than any practical use, has spent roughly 136 years twisting instead of growing straight, until arborists describe its 3.5-metre trunk as closer to a piece of vegetal sculpture than an ordinary shade tree. Every June its crown fills with white, orchid-patterned flowers in dense upright clusters, followed by the long, thin seed pods that earned the species its American nickname, the cigar tree. The Giardini della Guastalla itself predates almost everything else on this list: founded by Ludovica Torelli, Countess of Guastalla, as a garden for the girls' college she funded, it became one of Milan's first public parks open to all, four centuries after her death. At just over 12,000 square metres it is one of the smallest gardens on this list and one of the easiest to walk past, a few streets from the university hospital rather than fronting any grand piazza.
trees.access: Free, public garden (gated, roughly 7:00-21:00, hours vary seasonally)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Crocetta (M3)

best_time.label: June, when its white, orchid-like flowers cover the crown

trees.notes: The 136-year age figure comes from RAMI's registry only; independent sources confirm the tree, species and garden history but not that specific figure, so it is flagged as single-sourced.

trees.name: La Quercia Rossa di Piazza XXIV Maggio

location.address: Piazza XXIV Maggio, 20143 Milano

trees.story: This oak was already growing in an American nursery when Milan was still deciding what to do with the site of one of its six historic gates. Giunio Capè had the sapling brought to Piazza XXIV Maggio at the end of the First World War and planted it in 1924 in memory of his son Giuseppe, an Alpine soldier who survived the war, and of the Alpini who did not. A century later the oak stands nearly 20 metres tall with a trunk just under 5 metres around, held up since 2019 by a discreet steel exoskeleton a Bergamo carpentry firm built to support a crown that had begun to outgrow its own structure. Quercus rubra is native to eastern North America and turns a deep, almost oxidised red in October and November, the colour that gives the species its name and, briefly each autumn, the only real red in a square better known for the nineteenth century customs arches of the old Porta Ticinese behind it. Milanese press sometimes calls it the oldest tree in the city; it is not, several trees on this list are older, but it may be the only one whose exact planting date and reason for standing there are both on record.
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Porta Genova (M2), or tram 3/9/15 to Porta Ticinese

best_time.label: October and November, when its leaves turn a deep, oxidised red

trees.notes: The 'oldest tree in Milan' superlative repeated in some local press is not adopted here, per hard rule 8: the ginkgo pair at the Orto Botanico di Brera (mil_004) is considerably older and better documented. The 1924 planting/memorial story is corroborated by two independent press sources plus RAMI's registry entry.
trees.verify_notes: Height 18.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (3 m away).

trees.name: La Quercia Rossa del Trotter

location.address: Parco Trotter, Via Giacosa 46, 20127 Milano

trees.story: This oak grows on a horse-racing track that stopped racing a century ago and became a school instead. Parco Trotter takes its name from the Società del Trotter, which ran harness races here from the 1800s until the track moved to San Siro in 1924; when the sporting company folded, Milan's city council bought the abandoned oval and turned it, starting in 1919, into Casa del Sole, a 128,000 square metre open-air school for children with tuberculosis and other chronic illness, built on the belief that fresh air and space were themselves a treatment. The ring shape of the old racetrack still defines the park's paths today, cut across by a single straight avenue of plane trees. This red oak, planted not long after the school opened, now stands about 40 metres tall, taller than any other tree on this list, with a trunk 4.3 metres around, growing beside Via Giacosa near the park's old chapel. The school never fully closed. Children still attend classes on these grounds, which is why the park keeps unusual hours, open to the public only outside school time, free every day it opens rather than at any point in between.
trees.access: Free, public park, open outside school hours (times vary by season)
trees.transport: Bus or tram toward Loreto/Turro, then a short walk to Via Giacosa

best_time.label: October and November, when its canopy turns red above the old racetrack

trees.notes: Photo fetched and viewed directly 2026-07-28: a tall, mature tree with a substantial trunk towering over a park path with children and bicycles, the filename itself naming this exact park and species ('Parco Trotter, quercia rossa centenaria', centenarian red oak), consistent with this entry's own description of the tallest tree on the list.

trees.name: La Paulownia di Via Madonnina

location.address: Corner of Via Madonnina and Via San Carpoforo, 20121 Milano

trees.story: Milan's most photographed tree grows on a triangular scrap of land where a building once stood, until Allied bombs brought it down during the Second World War. Nothing was rebuilt on the corner of Via Madonnina and Via San Carpoforo, and sometime in the decades after the war a paulownia took root in the cleared gap, on land nobody had any particular plan for. By the 2010s the plot had become something else entirely: probably the most photographed tree in the city according to local press, its lilac flowers a fixture of every spring guide to the Brera district. That popularity is the only reason it still stands. A developer held rights to build a small residential block on the triangular lot, and only a sustained campaign by Brera residents, who formed a committee specifically to save the tree, persuaded Milan's city council to acquire the 155 square metre plot in 2016 in exchange for a larger site elsewhere in the city. The paulownia survived a violent storm in July 2023 that uprooted an old fig tree growing beside it. No scientific study has ever aged it precisely; residents describe it as over 65 years old, grown entirely on its own rather than planted by anyone with a plan.
trees.access: Free, visible from the street (small municipally-owned lot rather than a walk-in garden)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Lanza (M2)

best_time.label: April, when its lilac flowers cover the bare branches before the leaves appear

trees.notes: No individual tree registry entry found (this is a self-seeded tree on a former bomb site, not one of RAMI's catalogued specimens); age is press-reported ('over 65 years' as of 2023) rather than measured, and no exact planting date exists since nobody planted it deliberately. Coordinates are an estimate of the named street corner, not a surveyed point. Two Flickr photos of this exact tree were found and checked but both are marked All Rights Reserved, not a usable open licence.

trees.name: La Pianta di Affori
trees.age_estimate: 187 years by dendrochronological analysis; local tradition claims over 250

location.address: Corner of Viale Affori and Via Astesani, 20161 Milano

trees.story: Every Milanese from Affori knows this tree simply as la Pianta, the Plant, as if there were no other, and local legend insists Napoleon is the reason it stands where it does: supposedly planted to honour a Milanese noblewoman he had fallen for during his Italian campaign, sometime around 1800. Core samples taken in 2013, when a restoration crew drilled into the trunk to check its health, tell a more modest story: growth rings put the tree at about 187 years old at the time, closer to the 1820s than the Napoleonic Wars. This page gives both figures, since neither can be disproved outright and the drilled sample is the harder evidence. What is not in dispute is the tree itself: a plane 20 metres tall with a trunk over 2 metres in diameter, standing at the corner of Viale Affori and Via Astesani since before the surrounding neighbourhood existed as anything but farmland. An owl once nested in a cavity on its western side; the memory is marked today by a small wooden owl sculpture at the base of the trunk. A metal bracket further up the trunk, once used to string electrical cable through the branches, is a rare surviving trace of how Milan wired its outer suburbs before anyone thought to protect the tree carrying the load.
trees.access: Free, public street corner
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Affori Centro (M3)
trees.notes: Genuine age dispute between a 2013 dendrochronological core sample (about 187 years) and the popular Napoleonic-era legend (over 250 years); presented as a range with the scientific figure given more weight, per hard rule 8/P7. This is a different, still-living tree from the similarly aged plane at Villa Litta (also in Affori), which was felled in 2015 after a fungal disease; only a trunk cross-section of that one survives, noted in this city's FAQ rather than listed as a tree to visit. Pin corrected 2026-07-28, about 490m: Italy's volunteer-run RAMI tree registry (ilregistrodeglialberi.it) names this exact tree 'Platano di Affori' at Via Astesani, and OpenStreetMap/Nominatim independently geocodes 'Via Astesani, Affori' to within about 7m of RAMI's own coordinate, two independent sources converging tightly. Upgraded to confirmed.
trees.verify_notes: Height 20.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (5 m away).

trees.name: Il Noce del Caucaso di Parco Sempione

location.address: Parco Sempione, near the pond and Ponte delle Sirenette, 20154 Milano

trees.story: This walnut grows almost horizontally over the water, its lower limbs bending so far toward the pond in Parco Sempione that locals joke it is trying to drink from it. Pterocarya fraxinifolia is native to the Caucasus and northern Iran, a wetland species that thrives on constantly moist soil, exactly the condition it gets growing at the edge of the artificial lake beside the Ponte delle Sirenette, a footbridge moved here in 1930 when the canal it originally crossed elsewhere in Milan was filled in. Its trunk measures 4.35 metres around and 18 metres high, and Italy's monumental tree registry lists it, along with a second specimen 1.6 kilometres away in the Giardini Montanelli, as the oldest Caucasian walnut in the city, though no source gives either tree an exact age or planting date. Compound leaves, similar in shape to an ash tree's, turn a warm gold in October and November alongside the marsh cypresses planted at the same waterline, briefly making the pond's edge the best autumn colour anywhere in the park. Visitors headed for the Castello Sforzesco or the Triennale rarely detour the extra hundred metres to the water's edge where it grows.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cadorna (M1/M2) or Cairoli (M1)

best_time.label: October and November, when its foliage turns gold above the pond

trees.notes: No age or planting date documented anywhere found; age range is a wide, honest estimate from trunk girth and the park's 1893 redesign, not a measured figure.
trees.verify_notes: Height 18.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).

trees.name: Il Noce del Caucaso dell'Orto Botanico di Brera

location.address: Orto Botanico di Brera, arboreto, Via Brera 28, 20121 Milano

trees.story: The famous trees in this garden are the two ginkgos of 1775, and neither of them is the one the state decided to protect. That honour went to a Caucasian wingnut at the back of the arboretum, declared a monumental tree of Italy on 11 February 2025, the first tree in the Orto Botanico di Brera ever to carry the designation, granted in the year the garden turned 250. Pterocarya fraxinifolia comes from the forests between the Black Sea and northern Iran, where it grows in ground too wet for most hardwoods, and it behaves in Milan the way it behaves at home: instead of one clean column it throws its limbs sideways into a low green dome, with a root system spreading as wide as the crown. The national register measures the trunk at 4.7 metres around and the tree at 29 metres, which makes it the tallest of the three wingnuts standing in central Milan and the only one on university ground. Its age has never been established by ring count or planting record; the university says over eighty years, which is a floor rather than a figure. In summer it hangs chains of winged green seeds half a metre long from every branch, the detail that gives the genus its name, from the Greek for wing and nut.
trees.access: Free entry, Orto Botanico di Brera (Mon-Sat, hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Lanza (M2) or Montenapoleone (M3)

best_time.label: June and July, when half-metre chains of winged seeds hang from every branch

trees.notes: Species, dimensions and monumental status confirmed by two independent bodies: the national MASAF register (Pterocarya fraxinifolia, Orto Botanico di Brera, girth 470 cm, height 29 m) and the University of Milan's own announcement of the 11 February 2025 designation. Age is single-sourced and vague ('over 80 years', university press release); no ring count or planting record exists, so age_max is an honest upper bound from girth, not a figure anyone has published. Coordinates are the register's garden-level point, roughly 35 m from our own ginkgo entry (mil_004); the arboretum is at the back of the garden, so the pin is approximate rather than surveyed.
trees.verify_notes: Height 29.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).

trees.name: Il Platano della Biodiversita

location.address: Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, Via Palestro, 20121 Milano

trees.story: Milan picked one plane tree in this park and started counting what lives on it. The city's monumental tree file calls it simply Platano VTA 43474, and it was entered into a research cycle measuring how much biodiversity a single urban tree carries in its crown and on its bark: the beetles, lichens, mosses, spiders and birds that treat 30 metres of plane tree as an address. The answer, in a city of 170,000 street and park trees, turns out to be a lot, which is why a tree with no legend attached to it now has a municipal page of its own. It stands about 30 metres tall on a trunk 1.6 metres thick, and its roots do something planes often do in compacted parkland: instead of diving, they spread flat across the surface of the root plate like poured wax. The city built a low wooden fence around the base purely to keep service vehicles off them. Its main limbs join the trunk at weak, narrow angles, so rather than shorten them, arborists tied them back to the trunk with anchoring cables. Almost nobody walking the path notices either the fence or the cables, which is the point of both.
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Palestro (M1) or Porta Venezia (M1)
trees.notes: Two independent sources on existence, species and size: the Comune di Milano's own monumental-tree page (VTA inventory 43474, height 30 m, diameter at breast height 160 cm) and the national MASAF register (Platanus acerifolia, Giardini Indro Montanelli, girth 483 cm, height 32 m). Neither gives an age, and no planting record survives for this park, so the range is an honest estimate from girth alone. Pin is approximate on purpose: the two sources agree on latitude to five decimals but their longitudes sit about 165 m apart (register 9.200014, comune 9.197869), so the tree is somewhere along that line in the northern half of the gardens. Distinct from mil_002, the much wider 'grande' plane (830 cm girth) about 260 m south.
trees.verify_notes: Height 32.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).

trees.name: Il Noce del Caucaso dei Giardini Montanelli
trees.age_estimate: age undocumented, among the oldest of its species in Milan

location.address: Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, Corso Venezia 55, 20121 Milano

trees.story: Milan has three Caucasian wingnuts worth crossing town for, and this is the widest of them: 5.5 metres around, against 4.7 in the Brera botanical garden and 4.35 for the better-known specimen leaning over the pond in Parco Sempione. The city's own arborists pair this tree with the Sempione one as the two oldest of their species in Milan, which is as close to a date as anyone has put on either. It is a squat, wide, low tree rather than a tall one, 20 metres at most, because Pterocarya fraxinifolia spends its growth on width and on suckers: left alone it throws up new shoots from the base until a single tree reads as a thicket. Ash-like compound leaves, sometimes 60 centimetres long, turn butter yellow in late October. The species arrived in European gardens from the Caucasus and northern Iran in the early 1780s, brought back by a French botanist who found it growing in the wet forests south of the Caspian, and Milan planted it in parks for the same reason it planted bald cypress: land near ornamental water needed trees that would not sulk with wet feet. Walk the gardens' western edge toward Via Manin and it is the broad, many-stemmed one nobody photographs.
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours vary by season)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Turati (M3) or Palestro (M1)

best_time.label: late October, when the long compound leaves turn butter yellow

trees.notes: Existence, species and size from the national MASAF register (Pterocarya fraxinifolia, Giardini Indro Montanelli, girth 550 cm, height 20 m). The second source is the Comune di Milano's monumental-tree page for the Parco Sempione wingnut, which names this tree by the city's own inventory number ('Assieme a quella dei Giardini Montanelli, Pterocaria VTA 36443, e la pterocaria piu datata tra quelle presenti in citta'), confirming both its existence and its standing as one of the two oldest of its species in the city. No age figure exists anywhere; the range is an honest estimate from girth. Only one source publishes a coordinate, so the pin stays approximate. Photo downloaded and viewed at 960px this pass and approved against the Cadiz standard: the tree fills the frame in flat May daylight, the broad low crown and the multi-stemmed base are both readable, and the centre band of the card crop is all tree. Its description reads 'Caucasian wingnut, Giardini Pubblici, Milano' and its photographer, Sordelli, also took the hackberry photo already published on mil_003 in this same park; the file carries no geotag, but the register lists only one wingnut in these gardens, so the identification is safe. NOTE for a later pass: mil_010's story calls the Sempione wingnut's companion 'a companion specimen nearby', which the comune source shows is this tree, 1.6 km away in a different park, not a neighbour.
trees.verify_notes: Height 20.0 m from the italy-masaf register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).

trees.name: Il Platano del Giardino Bazlen

location.address: Giardino Roberto Bazlen e Luciano Foa, Corso di Porta Romana 106-116, 20122 Milano

trees.story: The garden is named after the two men who invented Adelphi, and the tree is the only thing in it older than the publishing house. Roberto Bazlen and Luciano Foa founded Adelphi Edizioni in Milan in 1962; the small green square off Corso di Porta Romana that carries their names is mostly a children's playground now, and this plane is the last big tree left standing in it. Its top was cut out at some point, which took metres off its height and left it stockier than it should be, but the trunk is still 1.95 metres thick, wide enough that the whole playground arranges itself around the base. The city is blunt about what happens next. Wood-decaying fungi have colonised the trunk and cannot be removed, so the tree is inspected at the collar and at every branch join, and the municipal page states plainly that it will be kept for as long as its presence does not create a safety problem over the play area beneath it. That is an unusually honest sentence to publish about a monument, and it is the reason to go now rather than eventually. Planes tolerate Milan's air better than almost anything else, which is how this one outlasted every other large tree on its own block.

trees.transport: 5 min walk from Crocetta (M3), or tram 16 along Corso di Porta Romana
trees.notes: Two independent sources: the Comune di Milano monumental-tree page (VTA 44854, trunk diameter 195 cm, crown reduced, fungal decay, periodic checks) and the national MASAF register (Platanus acerifolia, Giardino Roberto Balzen, Corso di Porta Romana 112-116, girth 600 cm, height 16 m; the register's spelling 'Balzen' is a typo for Bazlen). The two coordinates agree to within about 22 m, which is why this pin is confirmed rather than approximate. No age is published by either source; the range is estimated from girth. The tree is alive and monitored as of the comune page's last update, but its own manager says it stays only while it is safe above the playground, so a future pass should re-check before this entry ages.

trees.name: Il Platano Siamese di Villa Litta
trees.age_estimate: age undocumented, planted with the villa's 18th-century park

location.address: Parco di Villa Litta Modignani, Viale Affori 21, 20161 Milano

trees.story: Two plane trees grew close enough together here that they stopped being two. Their roots fused, then part of their trunks, then their crowns interlaced, and the result is catalogued by the city as one tree, Platano VTA 9595, nicknamed the Siamese. It reaches 34 metres, and the reason the city protects it has less to do with size than with occupancy. Colonies of ring-necked parakeets and starlings nest in its cavities, crows keep a nest in the crown, and until a few years ago the large hollow on the north trunk held a Great Grey Owl, a bird whose natural range is the boreal forest of Lapland and Siberia. Woodpeckers drill the trunk for the insect larvae that come with rotting heartwood, and those holes are also the clearest sign of what is happening inside: the city writes that the tree is at the end of its biological cycle, its internal decay advanced, its stability worse than it was, the heavy steel cables binding the two trunks together recently replaced. It stands 300 metres from the Pianta of Affori, in a park the Litta family laid out in the second half of the 1700s, and a visit is worth making sooner rather than later.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Affori FN (M3) or Affori Centro (M3)

best_time.label: January, when the leaves are off and the two fused trunks and their cables are fully visible

trees.notes: Existence, species, form and condition from the Comune di Milano's own monumental-tree page (VTA 9595, height 34 m, two fused trunks, cabled, described as at the end of its biological cycle) and the national MASAF register, which lists two surviving Villa Litta planes of 43 m and 38 m plus two further entries in the same park. Local history source milanoaffori.it independently confirms that plane trees planted in the second half of the 1700s still stand in this park. No source publishes an age for this specific tree, so the range is estimated from the park's own planting era, not measured. Coordinates: the comune's map point and the nearest register point differ by about 70 m, hence approximate. IMPORTANT: this is NOT the felled 1773 plane. That tree stood on the villa's south-east side until 2015 and its trunk section is displayed indoors; see data/leads/milan.json, blocked. Counted as ONE collectible point rather than two trees because the fusion is what the designation and the nickname are about, and there is one obvious place to stand. Photos: two CC BY-SA 4.0 Commons images of a Villa Litta plane exist (Platano comune a02.jpg and a03.jpg, Alberto Panzani, 2018), but both are geotagged at 45.515147, 9.166122, about 230 m from this tree and exactly on a different register entry, so neither can be used here.

trees.name: Il Platano di Piazza Sant'Ambrogio

location.address: Piazza Sant'Ambrogio / Largo Caduti Milanesi per la Patria, 20123 Milano

trees.story:
This plane tree joined Italy's national register of monumental trees in November 2025, which makes it one of the newest protected trees in the country and one of the taller ones in Milan. It stands 34 metres on a trunk 4.2 metres around, in the square in front of the Basilica di Sant'Ambrogio. Regione Lombardia announced it in a batch of 48 new entries that took the region's total to 476 recognised specimens.

Its age has never been published. Italy's national register carries girth and height and no field for years, and no city document or newspaper survey has filled the gap, so the only honest handle is size. A London Plane of this girth in Milan is usually somewhere in its second century, and the range given here is exactly that: an estimate read off a tape measure, not a record.

What it stands over is dated to the year. The basilica behind it was founded in 379 by Ambrose himself, and the low brick building with two unequal towers that you see today is the eleventh and twelfth-century replacement. Against that clock the tree is a newcomer. Against any other it is old.

It is also the tree most often photographed by accident in this city, sitting in the background of everybody's picture of the church, while being the reason the square has any shade at all.

trees.name: Il Platano di Viale Cervantes

location.address: Viale Cervantes, Parco Sempione, 20154 Milano

trees.story:
Parco Sempione is the most walked park in Milan, and this tree only entered the national register of monumental trees in November 2025. It stands on Viale Cervantes at 33 metres, on a trunk 3.9 metres around, one of 48 Lombard trees designated in a single announcement that took the region past 476 protected specimens.

Its age is not on record. Italy's register lists girth and height and leaves the years blank, and no local survey has ever dated this one, so the two numbers on the tape are the only figures that describe it honestly: 390 centimetres around, 33 metres up. Everything past that is inference from size, and inference is the right word for it.

Where it stands is more interesting than what it measures. Viale Cervantes runs through the park between the Castello Sforzesco at one end and the Arco della Pace at the other, which makes it a route rather than a destination, and almost everyone on it is going somewhere else. The same avenue carries the Caucasian Wingnut that bends out low over the park's pond, close enough that the two are a single short walk. Between them they make this stretch the part of Sempione worth slowing down for, which is not how most people use it. It is 33 metres of reason to stop.

trees.name: Il Platano dei 34 Metri ai Giardini Montanelli

location.address: Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli, Via Palestro, 20121 Milano

trees.story:
Depending on which document you trust, this is either one of the two tallest trees in Milan or simply one of the taller ones. Il Giorno's survey of the city's monumental trees calls 34 metres the greatest height reached by any plant in Milan and names two plane trees that get there, one at Villa Litta and this one, off via Palestro. Italy's national register separately lists a Villa Litta plane at 43 metres. The title is contested, and that is worth saying rather than picking a side.

The measurement of this tree is not contested: 475 centimetres around the trunk, 34 metres tall. Its age is blank. The national register has no field for years and no newspaper or municipal file has dated it, so girth and height are the only honest numbers here.

It is also not the famous tree in these gardens. That is the plane with the 8.36-metre trunk, dated to 239 years, which grew outwards into five limbs instead of upwards. This one did the opposite. It has a second registered plane nearby at 32 metres, plus a bald cypress, a Mediterranean hackberry and a Caucasian wingnut: six register-listed monumental trees inside one set of railings, in a park first laid out in 1784.

Nobody stops for this one, because in company like that, being the tallest is not conspicuous. Look up rather than at the trunk.
verified_sources: MASAF national register, sheet 11/F205/MI/03, Giardini Indro Montanelli - Corso Venezia (Platanus acerifolia, girth 475 cm, height 34 m)

https://www.ilgiorno.it/milano/cronaca/alberi-monumentali-1.7590565 (Il Giorno, 'Verde, sono 17 gli alberi monumentali a Milano', quoting verbatim: 'un altro platano, anche in questo caso ai Giardini Montanelli di via Palestro' reaching the same 34-metre height as the Villa Litta plane, described as the tallest plant height in the city)

trees.name: The Archdevil of Villa Marietti Radice Fossati

location.address: Villa Marietti Radice Fossati, piazza Villapizzone 3, Milano

trees.story:
The comune's own page for this hackberry calls it arcidiavolo, the archdevil, after a folk tale that blamed its hooked leaves on Lucifer, said to have carried the species down from heaven clutched in his claws. The city's monumental-tree list is usually a good deal drier than that.

The tree stands in the park of Villa Marietti Radice Fossati, in Villapizzone, northwest of the centre. The villa was given its rural character by the Radice Fossati family, fell into disrepair through the 1970s, and was pulled back out of it by a small experimental community of Jesuit fathers. The Comune di Milano took ownership in 1993 and confirmed the community's loan of the buildings, which have been residential ever since. So the buildings are somebody's home and the park around them is not, and the city says plainly that with the discretion due to an inhabited place you may pass through the gate and visit the park.

The trunk measures 4.2 metres round and the crown spreads more than 20 metres, throwing shade over roughly 200 square metres by the comune's reckoning. Its roots, structure and vegetative state are all recorded as good, and nothing on record says the tree has ever needed work. Nobody has published an age for it, only that girth, among the largest for the species anywhere in Milan.
verified_sources: MASAF national register, Milano, Villa Marietti Radice Fossati (Celtis australis, girth 420 cm, height 18 m)
trees.access: Free. The villa buildings are a lived-in community and the park around them is not: the Comune di Milano, which owns the villa, states on its own page for this tree that with the discretion due to an inhabited place you may pass through the gate and visit the park.
trees.transport: Short walk from Milano Villapizzone railway station
trees.notes:
BLOCKER of 2026-08-17 answered rather than obeyed, and the reviewer was right to raise it. It read the entry as a courtyard of a dwelling under hard rule 10's absolute home test. The premise was OUR OWN invented sentence: the first version of this story said the villa's inner courtyard is 'square, arcaded on three sides, and the hackberry stands at the centre of it', which no source says. It is a bridge claim of exactly the kind the corpus names, and as usual the join decided the LOCATION. The comune's own page describes a park and says 'e' possibile varcare il cancello per visitare il parco', it is possible to pass through the gate to visit the park, with the discretion due to an inhabited place. That is the landowner, the Comune di Milano itself, stating that visitors are admitted, which is what hard rule 10 asks for. The buildings are the home; the park is not.

Two location errors fixed in the same pass, found by reading that page in a browser session because comune.milano.it 403s every plain fetcher. The address said Via Villapizzone 9 and the comune says piazza Villapizzone 3. The pin sat 83 metres from the comune's own marker while claiming 'confirmed'; it now uses the comune's coordinate and says approximate, because that marker is the villa rather than the trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: A very wide hackberry in the villa park, crown spreading over 20 metres. The pin is the comune's own marker for the villa rather than the trunk, so expect to look once you are inside the gate.

trees.name: Il Platano di Viale Montesanto

location.address: Viale Montesanto 4/6, Milano

trees.story:
A newspaper survey of Milan's monumental trees once put the city's ceiling at 34 metres. Italy's national register disagrees in several places, and this plane is one of them: 38 metres, growing at a street number rather than in a park.

It stands outside Viale Montesanto 4 to 6, on the ring of boulevards that traces the line of Milan's sixteenth-century Spanish walls, on the stretch between Porta Garibaldi and the Giardini Montanelli. The register gives the trunk at 5.25 metres round. The city's celebrated plane, the Platano di Indro in the Giardini Montanelli, carries 8.36 metres and spent it going sideways into five limbs. This one had a pavement, a road and a row of facades, so it went up.

Nobody has published an age for it. The national register carries girth and height and keeps no field for years, and no municipal file or local survey has filled the gap for this particular tree, so the tape measure is the only evidence there is. If you know when this stretch of the viale was planted, tell us and we will say so.

There is no gate and no opening time. You walk the pavement to number 4 and look up until the crown closes over the road.

trees.name: Il Platano di Piazzale Libia

location.address: Piazzale Libia, Milano

trees.story:
Milan's best known plane trees stop at 34 metres. This one is 35, and it is standing in the middle of a traffic square.

Piazzale Libia lies about a kilometre out from Porta Romana in the south-east of the city, a junction broad enough to have kept room in the middle of it for a tree this size. Italy's national register of monumental trees lists the plane there at 35 metres on a trunk 4 metres round. That is taller than the register's own entry for the plane in front of the Basilica di Sant'Ambrogio and taller than the one in the Giardini Montanelli that a local survey named among the tallest plants in Milan.

Street planes almost never get the chance. Across Italy they are cut back on a cycle to clear the wires and the balconies, and a plane that has been topped does not come back to a height like this. Whatever else was done to this tree, nobody took its crown out.

Its age is not recorded anywhere. The national register measures girth and height and stops there, and no other document names this tree at all, so the years are simply missing. Anyone who knows when the square was planted can close that gap for us.

Nothing to pay and nothing to open. Cross at the lights, stand under it, and work out how much of the sky it is holding up.

trees.name: The Plane of Viale Vittorio Veneto 3

location.address: Viale Vittorio Veneto 3, Milano

verified_sources: Italian national register of monumental trees (MASAF), Milano, Viale Vittorio Veneto 3
trees.access: Free, street tree on the public boulevard (Bastioni) near Porta Venezia.
trees.transport: About 300 m northeast of the Giardini Indro Montanelli cluster, on foot.
trees.story:
A story went round Milan in 2018 that the big plane on Viale Vittorio Veneto, growing in the old tram-line median near Porta Venezia, had dried out and been cut down. It probably wasn't this one. That felled tree measured about three metres round; this one, still standing at the same address, measures 5.70 metres, nearly double, too large a gap to be the same trunk misremembered. The register lists this plane as one of the largest in the city by girth, 36 metres tall.

Viale Vittorio Veneto runs along the Bastioni, the boulevard laid over Milan's old Spanish city walls after they came down, three hundred metres from the plane trees and monuments of the Giardini Indro Montanelli. No source beyond the register names this specific tree, so its age and any history particular to it stay unrecorded.

It grows as a street tree on the public boulevard, free to see at any hour, no gate and no ticket. If you know anything about its planting, or about the tree that really was felled here in 2018, tell us.
